title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK
objective: Number and rank rows within groups, choose the right function for ties, and use ranking to answer top-N-per-group, latest-record-per-entity and de-duplication questions.
context: 'Top 2 products in every category', 'each customer's latest order', 'remove duplicate rows from the load' — the same window pattern answers all three. In Snowflake you'll write it with QUALIFY; here you'll write the portable version with a CTE.

exercises.title: Rank products by units sold
exercises.question: Merchandising wants a units-sold leaderboard where tied products share a position.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders are order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'). For every product sold in a valid order, return product_id, units_sold (SUM(quantity)) and units_rank = RANK() by units_sold descending (ties share a rank; highest = 1).
hints: Aggregate units per product first.
RANK() OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC) — no tie-breaker on purpose, so ties share a rank.
WITH units AS (SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold ... GROUP BY oi.product_id) SELECT product_id, units_sold, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC) AS units_rank FROM units;
exercises.why: Leaderboards must treat ties fairly; RANK is the 'sports table' convention (1, 2, 2, 4).
exercises.snowflake: Identical; you can also rank directly on the aggregate: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity) DESC) in the GROUP BY query.

exercises.title: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
exercises.question: An analyst wants to see how the three ranking functions treat customers with equal order counts.
exercises.prompt: Valid orders are order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'). For every customer_id that has valid orders (including the orphan 99), return customer_id, order_count (number of valid orders), row_num (ROW_NUMBER by order_count descending, then customer_id ascending), rnk (RANK by order_count descending) and dense_rnk (DENSE_RANK by order_count descending).
hints: Count valid orders per customer in a CTE.
Three window functions, same ORDER BY order_count DESC; only ROW_NUMBER needs the customer_id tie-breaker.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY order_count DESC, customer_id) AS row_num, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY order_count DESC) AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY order_count DESC) AS dense_rnk
exercises.why: Choosing the wrong ranking function silently changes 'top 3' results whenever there are ties.

recall.q: Which function never produces gaps but does produce ties?

exercises.title: Each customer's most recent order
exercises.question: Customer success wants each customer's latest order (any status) for their account view.
exercises.prompt: For every customer_id in orders (any status, including the orphan 99), return customer_id, order_id, order_date and order_status of that customer's most recent order (latest order_date; if two share a date, the higher order_id). Use ROW_NUMBER.
hints: PARTITION BY customer_id; ORDER BY order_date DESC so the latest is row 1.
Add order_id DESC as tie-breaker, then keep rn = 1 in an outer query.

WITH ranked AS (SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn FROM orders) SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, order_status FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
exercises.why: MAX(order_date) gives the date but not the rest of the row. 'Latest row per entity' is the most common ROW_NUMBER use in data engineering (SCDs, snapshots, CDC).

recall.q: Why not just SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date), order_status ... GROUP BY customer_id?
recall.a: order_status isn't aggregated, so it's not guaranteed to come from the latest row (and Snowflake rejects it).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, order_status FROM orders QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;

exercises.title: Top 2 products per category
exercises.question: Each category manager wants their two best-selling products by revenue.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. For each category (exclude NULL category), return the top 2 products by product_revenue: category, product_id, product_name, product_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and rank_in_category (ROW_NUMBER within the category by product_revenue descending, then product_id ascending). Only rows with rank_in_category <= 2.
hints: Step 1: revenue per (category, product). Step 2: rank within category. Step 3: filter.
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id).

WITH product_rev AS (...GROUP BY p.category, p.product_id, p.product_name), ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, product_id) AS rank_in_category FROM product_rev) SELECT ... WHERE rank_in_category <= 2;
exercises.why: Top-N per group is impossible with plain GROUP BY + LIMIT (LIMIT applies to the whole result). PARTITION BY + ROW_NUMBER is the standard answer.

recall.q: Why doesn't ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 2 give top 2 per category?
recall.a: LIMIT applies to the whole result, not per group.

exercises.snowflake: ... GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, p.product_id) <= 2;

exercises.title: Find duplicate order lines
exercises.question: Data engineering found duplicate-looking order lines. Which rows should be deleted (keep the earliest of each set)?
exercises.prompt: Treat order lines with the same order_id, product_id, quantity and unit_price as duplicates. Within each duplicate set, keep the row with the lowest order_item_id. Return order_item_id, order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price and kept_order_item_id (the lowest order_item_id of that set) for every row that would be removed.
hints: PARTITION BY every column that defines 'the same line'.
ROW_NUMBER ordered by order_item_id: rn = 1 is the keeper, rn > 1 are duplicates. MIN(order_item_id) over the same partition names the keeper.

ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price ORDER BY order_item_id) AS rn, MIN(order_item_id) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price) AS kept_order_item_id ... WHERE rn > 1
exercises.why: ROW_NUMBER-based dedup is how pipelines clean double-loaded data. Listing the rows to remove (with their keeper) before deleting is the safe workflow.

recall.q: In ROW_NUMBER dedup, what goes in PARTITION BY and what in ORDER BY?
recall.a: PARTITION BY the columns that define a duplicate; ORDER BY the rule that picks the keeper (e.g. lowest id / latest load).

exercises.snowflake: SELECT * FROM order_items QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price ORDER BY order_item_id) > 1; To rebuild a clean table: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE ... AS SELECT * FROM order_items QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1;

exercises.title: Top 2 customers per region (tie-safe)
exercises.question: Regional sales leads want their top customers — if two customers tie, both should be listed.
exercises.prompt: Gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over the order_items of valid orders (order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')); cancelled and pending orders are excluded. Per customer (customers table, region not NULL), compute gross revenue. Within each region, rank customers with DENSE_RANK by gross revenue descending and keep those with region_rank <= 2. Return region, customer_id, name, gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) and region_rank.
hints: Revenue per customer (with region) in a CTE; inner joins drop customers without valid orders.
DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY gross_revenue DESC) — no tie-breaker, so ties share a rank.

... ranked AS (SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY gross_revenue DESC) AS region_rank FROM cust_rev) SELECT region, customer_id, name, ROUND(gross_revenue, 2) AS gross_revenue, region_rank FROM ranked WHERE region_rank <= 2;
exercises.why: 'Top 2' is ambiguous with ties: ROW_NUMBER gives exactly 2 rows, RANK/DENSE_RANK can give more. Decide (and document) which the business wants.

recall.q: You need 'top 3 including ties'. ROW_NUMBER or RANK?
recall.a: RANK (or DENSE_RANK for top 3 distinct values) — ROW_NUMBER cuts ties arbitrarily.

exercises.snowflake: ... GROUP BY 1, 2, 3 QUALIFY DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.region ORDER BY gross_revenue DESC) <= 2;

exercises.title: Days between first and second order
exercises.question: Retention team: for customers who came back, how many days passed between their first and second valid order?
exercises.prompt: Valid orders are order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'). Number each customer's valid orders with ROW_NUMBER by order_date, then order_id. For customer_ids in orders with at least 2 valid orders, return customer_id, first_order_date, second_order_date and days_between (integer days from first to second order).
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id) gives each order its sequence number.
Pivot sequence 1 and 2 onto one row with MAX(CASE WHEN order_seq = 1 THEN order_date END) ... GROUP BY customer_id.
... then CAST(julianday(second_order_date) - julianday(first_order_date) AS INTEGER) AS days_between ... WHERE second_order_date IS NOT NULL
exercises.why: Order sequence numbers unlock repeat-purchase metrics: time to 2nd order, first-order vs repeat revenue, cohort behaviour (Module 4, second half).

recall.q: How do you get 'the nth event per customer'?
recall.a: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY event time, tie-breaker) and filter/pivot on the number.

exercises.snowflake: Same pattern; or NTH_VALUE(order_date, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) with DATEDIFF(day, first, second).

worked_example.question: Show ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK side by side for products 15, 19, 17 and 9 by units sold (valid orders).
worked_example.sql:
WITH units AS (
    SELECT oi.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold
    FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
      AND oi.product_id IN (9, 15, 17, 19)
    GROUP BY oi.product_id
)
SELECT product_id,
       units_sold,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC, product_id) AS row_num,
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC)             AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY units_sold DESC)             AS dense_rnk
FROM units
ORDER BY units_sold DESC, product_id;
worked_example.explanation: Products 15 and 19 both sold 19 units: ROW_NUMBER breaks the tie by product_id (2, 3), RANK gives both 2 and skips 3 (next is 4), DENSE_RANK gives both 2 and continues with 3.

recipe:
**Recipe: rank → filter in 3 moves**

1. **Rank inside the window**:
   `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY measure DESC, tie_breaker)`
   - `ROW_NUMBER` → 1,2,3,4 — always unique (needs a tie-breaker to be deterministic).
   - `RANK` → 1,2,2,4 — ties share a rank, then a gap.
   - `DENSE_RANK` → 1,2,2,3 — ties share a rank, no gap.
2. **Wrap it** in a CTE/subquery (window functions can't go in WHERE).
3. **Filter outside**: `WHERE rn = 1` (latest / dedup), `WHERE rn <= 3` (top 3 exactly),
   `WHERE rnk <= 3` (top 3 *including ties*).

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                              ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
    FROM orders o
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;   -- latest order per customer
```
snowflake_notes:
Snowflake's **QUALIFY** filters on window functions directly — no wrapping CTE:

```sql
-- latest order per customer
SELECT *
FROM orders
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1;

-- top 2 products per category by revenue
SELECT p.category, p.product_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS product_revenue
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products p     ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
GROUP BY 1, 2
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category ORDER BY product_revenue DESC, p.product_id) <= 2;
```

Evaluation order in Snowflake: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → **window functions → QUALIFY** → ORDER BY → LIMIT.
Related: `MAX_BY(order_id, order_date)` returns the order_id with the latest date (one value per group),
`NTILE(4)` buckets into quartiles, `PERCENT_RANK()` gives 0–1 positions. SQLite supports NTILE and PERCENT_RANK too.
common_mistakes: ROW_NUMBER without a unique tie-breaker — the 'winner' among ties can change between runs.
Filtering a window result in WHERE of the same query — not allowed; wrap it (or use QUALIFY in Snowflake).
Using ROW_NUMBER when ties should both be kept (or RANK when exactly N rows are required).
Forgetting PARTITION BY, so 'top 2 per category' becomes 'top 2 overall'.
Using MAX(date) + GROUP BY to fetch 'the latest row' and then selecting non-aggregated columns.
Deduplicating on too few columns — always list every column that defines 'the same record'.
recall: Values 50, 40, 40, 30 ordered DESC: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK?
Snowflake one-liner for 'latest order per customer'?
QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) = 1
Where does QUALIFY run in the logical order?
After window functions (after HAVING), before ORDER BY/LIMIT.
Pattern for top-N per group in SQLite?
CTE with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY measure DESC, tie_breaker), outer WHERE rn <= N.
